how do you trust your agents' work more? copy this post/link and give it to your @bot or agent!

1. codebase improvements: this is just good software engineering - better architecture, stronger types and invariants, clear boundaries. agents love to copy what exists and take the shortest path, so make the easy thing the right thing. categorically eliminate problems through code and you won't need to think about it again.
2. static analysis: lint rules, tests, CI, verification (eg TLA+). very token efficient ways to catch issues ahead of time.
3. prose: comments, rules, AGENTS.md, skills - anything that can't be enforced and requires agent judgment. use it minimally, but do use /create-verification-skill.
4. human review: the hardest to scale. at the rate agents land code, it's pretty much impossible to thoroughly review every PR, so spend that effort on the highest leverage point, designing an environment where agents do the right thing by default.

this forms an inverse pyramid: you want most of your effort at the top, least at the bottom. codebase improvements are deterministic, making it more token efficient, and lets you sleep more soundly at night.

install https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack and create a new Project:
1. look through my slack/chat messages and code review comments where i've given feedback on PRs, code, architecture
2. use /recall on my past transcripts to learn how i steer agents
3. /poteto-mode use /correct and /architect on past commits to find the most common pitfalls agents fall into, then propose a plan to rearchitect the code i own so it's more agent friendly. answer open questions with prototyping rather than defer to me, and back the plan with real data. 
4. before you begin, use /sharpen + /in-your-own-words and confirm this prompt with me

Can I be real for a sec? I'm super nervous about this launch. It's something I never thought I would do, and I want to be as transparent as possible.

This course is $1,300. You should not buy it. Let me explain.

I've done YouTube for over 5 years now. I've never done a paid course of any form before. I have worked hard to keep all of my content freely available.

I'm lucky to have found so many awesome companies that will sponsor short sections of my videos, enabling me to employ an incredible team without compromising my content.

I have always hated the idea of charging my viewers. If I can't convince a company to cover our costs, that's my failure, and I don't like putting that failure on my audience.

On October 26th, my first-ever paid course with @megadevhq goes live. It's $1300 a seat. That's really expensive.

I keep imagining a scenario and it makes me feel sick. I think of a young, excited dev who's recently gotten into my content. They're scared of falling behind, so they cut their expenses and save up the money, because they believe my course might be the key to getting a real dev job.

Even now as I type this, I feel my heart rate increasing and my stomach flipping over itself. The thought of anyone putting themselves in a harder financial position, all because of me?

This might actually be my biggest fear.

I don't want to sell promises. I don't want people paying me for hope.

So why did I do this course with Mega?

Two reasons: the people and the content.

I was hit up by Joel about this course late last year. I trust him with my life. Even then, it wouldn't have been enough to convince me.

Then I learned the other instructors who would be involved. Kent, Angie and John. All three were fundamental in my growth as an engineer. Getting to work with all of them was far too exciting. Made it really hard to say no.

If I had nothing unique to say, I still would have said no. I'm incredibly busy as-is, and I'm running low on space to even show you guys all the stuff I do.

What pushed me over the line was the realization that there is so much I want to say that doesn't fit in a YouTube video.

I just did a video about "prompting better". It's a deep dive on my real world workflows and how I think about building with AI. The only way I could get people to watch it was clickbaiting the title, "your prompts suck".

What if I wasn't bound by clickability? What if I didn't have to focus on being entertaining for the whole video runtime? What if I was freed from the constrains of making content for the 500,000+ people who watch my videos?

I love YouTube. I love my audience. I love the videos I make. But I'd also love to do a multi-part deep dive on "building with AI in real world code bases" that I know would bomb on YouTube.

That's what I filmed for Mega. I'm so proud of it. It's fundamentally different from any videos I've done before, but still feels like me just doing my thing.

Is it worth $1,300, though? If that $1,300 comes out of the same bank account that you pay rent with, probably not.

Is it worth $1,300 per person to a company trying to help their eng teams use AI properly at work? In my opinion, this is a bargain.

If you're paying your engineers $100k a year, and this course makes them 5% more effective at their jobs, that's a 4x ROI.

What I'm trying to say is simple: Don't buy this course.

Get your boss to buy it.

(If you have an education budget at your job that works too. Just please don't pay for this yourself. Seriously.)

Sorry for the rant. If you can't tell, I'm genuinely quite nervous about this 🙃

Obligatory call out:
Yes, the course is expensive. That's because we want your company/boss to pay for it.

If you can't expense it, please do NOT buy this course if you aren't making Real Dev Money™.

It's super focused on "how to apply your existing engineering knowledge to building with AI". Genuinely not that useful if you're not a full time dev yet.

Seriously: DO NOT PUT YOURSELF IN A BAD FINANCIAL POSITION TO TAKE THIS COURSE. My free YouTube videos will help you more with getting your first job, I promise 🙏

linked_earlier_context.text:
T3 Connect has not been reliable today. Super sorry about that. Should be recovered now 🤞

Nerdy deets below for those who care:

T3 Connect is our built-in alternative to Tailscale for remote connections on T3 Code.

Turns out there's so many T3 Connect users that we are hitting some rate limits on Cloudflare's side! They have confirmed the issues on their end and are working on fixes.

We were unaware of these limits (seems like they were too). We're well under the limits we knew about, specifically the # of tunnels we can deploy to our users. The alerting on these failures was also pretty rough. CF has confirmed all of this and is working on fixes on their end 🙏

Crazy to have a product so popular that it's taking down CloudFlare lol. We are working hard to prevent these types of regressions going forward.

This work is full of fun challenges. Once a thundering herd starts, we're a bit screwed since we can't control the code you're running on your end! We have to plan way in advance for changes because we can't guarantee that users are on the latest version at any given time.

Thanks for sticking through with us in the interim. If you want to maximize your uptime and minimize chances of connection loss like today, I will not be disappointed if you set up Tailscale as a fallback (I do this personally)
